newsitem.title: USA: AMR sees Q3 costs higher, BA pact delay.
newsitem.headline: AMR sees Q3 costs higher, BA pact delay.

text.p: AMR Corp chief executive Robert Crandall said on Tuesday slow progress in open-skies talks between the U.S. and the United Kingdom are likely to cause a delay in implementing the airline's alliance with British Airways Plc.
Saying the process has taken considerably longer than expected, Crandall said, "It is clear our original timetable will slip."
Crandall also said costs per available seat mile would rise slightly less than four per cent in the third quarter.
"Fuel prices have come in much higher than we had expected," said Crandall, who was speaking at a breakfast hosted by the Society of Airline Analysts.
Higher fuel prices accounted for more than half of the increase in costs per seat mile for the quarter, he said.

Despite the fuel and other extra costs -- including AMR's share of costs to settle a suit by travel agents over commission caps as well as higher security costs and profit sharing accruals -- the quarter stands to be another good one for the company, Crandall said.
"The third quarter will be a good one," he said. "It just will not be as strong as we would have liked."
He said ticket demand held up despite re-imposition of a 10 percent federal excise tax, passed on via a fare increase.
"Our advance bookings are ahead of where they were a year ago," Crandall said.
Crandall also said the company planned to use free cash flow to rehabilitate its balance sheet with the goal of restoring the company to investment grade credit status.
Once that goal were achieved, he said, the company would likely give serious consideration to share repurchases.

Growing airline operations quickly is not an option, he said, because its American Airlines unit failed to win concessions in recently-concluded pilot talks that would have allowed it to carve out a low-cost short-haul service.
Because of that failure and the fact that American's fleet is relatively young, he said, AMR's needs for new aircraft "should be quite modest for some years."
He said capital spending would likely be focused on building American's international business, with the addition of "a modest number" of Boeing Co 757's possible.
